[[File:Equisetum arvense fertile spore-bearing stem - Keila.jpg|thumb|Fertile shoot]]
'''''Equisetum arvense''''', commonly known as '''field horsetail''' or '''common horsetail''', is a [[species]] of [[vascular plant]] in the horsetail [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Equisetaceae]]. Like all horsetails, it is a type of [[fern]]. It is native throughout the [[arctic]] and [[temperate]] regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. It has two distinct growth forms, a fertile [[spore]]-bearing stem and a sterile green stem. It is sometimes confused with mare's tail, ''[[Hippuris vulgaris]]''.

==Description==
''Equisetum arvense'' is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous plant]] that spreads by means of an underground [[rhizome]]. The slender, felted rhizome freely forks and bears [[stem tuber]]s. The species is [[wikt:dimorphic|dimorphic]], that is, it exhibits two distinct growth forms, both arising from the same rhizome. [[wikt:fertile|Fertile]] [[spore]]-bearing stems begin to appear in April. After shedding its spores, a fertile stem promptly withers and dies. [[wikt:sterile|Sterile]] green stems appear around the same time but last throughout the summer until the first frosts of autumn.{{r|Hyde-1978|FNA:233500616|MichFlora}}

The erect or prostrate sterile stems are {{convert|10–90|cm|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|3–5|mm|abbr=on}} diameter, with jointed segments around {{convert|2–5|cm|abbr=on}} long with whorls of side shoots at the segment joints; the side shoots have a diameter of about {{convert|1|mm|abbr=on}}. Some stems can have as many as 20 segments. The solid and simple branches are ascending or spreading, with sheaths that bear [[wikt:attenuate|attenuate]] teeth. The off-white fertile stems are of a [[succulent]] texture, {{convert|10–25|cm|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|3–5|mm|abbr=on}} diameter, with 4–8 whorls of brown scale leaves and an apical brown spore cone. The cone is {{convert|10–40|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4–9|mm|abbr=on}} broad.{{r|Hyde-1978}} The fertile stems are typically precocious and appear in early spring.<ref name="Fernald-1970">{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author= Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year= 1970 |editor= R. C. Rollins |publisher= D. Van Nostrand Company |edition= Eighth (Centennial) – Illustrated|isbn= 0-442-22250-5 |page= 4}}</ref> It has changed little from its ancestors of the [[Carboniferous]] period.

''E. arvense'' is a nonflowering plant, multiplying through spores. It absorbs silicon from the soil, which is rare among herbs.{{citation needed|date=March 2020}} It has a very high [[diploid]] number of 216 (108 pairs of chromosomes).{{r|Hyde-1978}}

==Taxonomy==
[[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] [[species description|describe]]d field horsetail with the [[binomial nomenclature|binomial]] ''Equisetum arvense'' in his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' of 1753.<ref>{{cite book | title=Species Plantarum | edition=1st | volume=II | last=Linnaeus | first=C. | authorlink=Carl Linnaeus | year=1753 | publisher=Laurentii Salvii | location=Stockholm | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/359082|page=1061}}</ref> The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''arvense'' is from the [[Latin language|Latin]] "arvum", meaning "arable land", referring to the growth of the plant in arable soil or disturbed areas. The common name "common horsetail" references the appearance of the plant that when bunched together appears similar to a horse's tail.{{r|Parsons-2001}}

Many species of horsetail have been described and subsequently synonymized with ''E. arvense''. One of these is ''E. calderi'', a small form described from Arctic North America.<ref>{{cite journal | last= Boivin | first= Bernard | date= January–March 1960 |title= A New Equisetum | journal= American Fern Journal |  volume= 50 | issue= 1 | pages= 107–109 | doi= 10.2307/1545251 | jstor= 1545251 | bibcode= 1960AmFJ...50..107B | url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/230177 }}</ref>

===Names===
Some other common names include '''bottle-brush''', '''devil's-guts''', '''foxtail-rush''', '''horse pipes''', '''horsetail fern''', '''meadow-pine''', '''pine-grass''', and '''snake-grass'''.<ref>{{cite web |title=field horsetail ''Equisetum arvense'' Weed Profile |url=https://weedid.cals.vt.edu/profile/73 |website=Weed Identification - Virginia Cooperative Extension |publisher=College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Virginia Tech |access-date=8 March 2024 |language=en}}</ref>
It is also known as '''marestail''', primarily in the UK,<ref>{{cite web |title=Field horsetail |url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/how-to/solve-problems/field-horsetail/ |website=BBC Gardeners World Magazine |access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref> but this common name is also used for the flowering aquatic plant ''[[Hippuris vulgaris]]'' and the common North American weed ''[[Erigeron canadensis]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hotchkiss |first1=Neil |title=Common Marsh, Underwater, and Floating-leaved Plants of the United States and Canada |date=1972 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=978-0-486-22810-5 |page=60 |url=https://archive.org/details/commonmarshunder0000hotc/page/60 |access-date=8 March 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Smith-Fiola |first1=Deborah |last2=Gill |first2=Stanton |title=Marestail: Identification and Management in Nursery and Landscape Settings |url=https://extension.umd.edu/resource/marestail-identification-and-management-nursery-and-landscape-settings |website=University of Maryland Extension |access-date=8 March 2024 |date=2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Equisetum arvense'' grows in a wide range of conditions, in temperatures less than {{convert|5|C|abbr=on}} to greater than {{convert|20|C|abbr=on}} and in areas that receive annual rainfall as low as {{convert|100|mm|abbr=on}} and as great as {{convert|2000|mm|abbr=on}}. It commonly occurs in damp and open woodlands, pastures, arable lands, roadsides, disturbed areas, and near the edge of streams. It prefers neutral or slightly basic clay [[loam]]s that are sandy or silty, especially where the water table is high, though it can occur occasionally on slightly acid soils.{{r|Parsons-2001}}

The plant is widespread in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], growing as far as 83° North in [[North America]] and 71° North in [[Norway]], [[Sweden]], [[Finland]], and [[Russia]] and as far south as [[Texas]], [[India]] and [[Iran]]. It is less widespread in the [[Southern Hemisphere]], but it occurs in [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[Chile]], [[Madagascar]], [[Indonesia]], and [[Australia]].{{r|Parsons-2001}} It was introduced into [[New Zealand]] in the 1920s where it was identified as an [[Invasive species in New Zealand|invasive species]] by [[Ella Orr Campbell]] in 1949.<ref name="Clemens-2003">{{cite journal|last1=Clemens|first1=J|title=In Memory of Ella O. Campbell, DNZM, FRIH|journal=Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture|year=2003|volume=6|issue= 1 |page=2 |url=https://www.rnzih.org.nz/RNZIH_Journal/Page2_from_2003_Vol6_No1.pdf|accessdate=14 March 2015}}</ref> It is listed on the [[National Pest Plant Accord]], prohibiting its sale, spread and cultivation.<ref>{{cite book|last=Howell|first=Clayson|title=Consolidated list of environmental weeds in New Zealand|publisher=Department of Conservation|location=Wellington|date=May 2008|series=DRDS292|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf|isbn=978-0-478-14413-0|accessdate=2009-05-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530024209/http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf|archive-date=30 May 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
''Equisetum arvense'' is toxic to livestock, particularly horses.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://research.vet.upenn.edu/PoisonousPlantsofPA/Equisetumarvense/tabid/5438/Default.aspx |title=Equisetum arvense |work=Poisonous Plants of Pennsylvania |accessdate=3 March 2018 |archive-date=3 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180303110624/http://research.vet.upenn.edu/PoisonousPlantsofPA/Equisetumarvense/tabid/5438/Default.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is difficult to control due to its extensive underground [[rhizome]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oregonstate.edu/dept/nursery-weeds/weedspeciespage/horsetail/Equisetum_arvense_horsetail.html|title=Equisetum arvense horsetail|website=oregonstate.edu|access-date=2020-03-06|archive-date=14 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181114181423/http://oregonstate.edu/dept/nursery-weeds/weedspeciespage/horsetail/Equisetum_arvense_horsetail.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> which can penetrate the soil up to {{convert|6|ft}} deep. Fire, mowing, or slashing are ineffective since new stems quickly grow from the rhizomes. Some [[herbicide]]s remove aerial growth but regrowth quickly occurs albeit with a reduction in [[frond]] density.{{r|Parsons-2001}}

==Uses==
[[File:Equisetum arvense fertile.png|thumb|100px|Drawing of a fertile stem of ''E. arvense'', 10 cm as drawn. At the top is the [[strobilus]], which consists of the axis (inside) and 15–20 horizontal circles of about 20 sporangiophores. Lower on the stem are two sheaths of merged [[microphyll]]s. The stem has many strong lengthwise ridges.]]

=== Medicine ===
The plant contains several substances that can be used medicinally. It is rich in [[silicon]] (2-3%),{{cn|date=October 2025}} [[potassium]], [[calcium]], manganese, magnesium and phosphorus, [[phytosterol]]s, dietary fiber, vitamins A, E and C, tannins, alkaloids, saponins, flavonoids, glycosides and caffeic acid phenolic ester. The buds are eaten as a [[vegetable]] in [[Japan]] and [[Korea]] in [[Spring (season)|spring]]. All other ''[[Equisetum]]'' species are toxic.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}} In polluted conditions{{Citation needed|date=December 2010}}, it may synthesize [[nicotine]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Bebbington|first=A|title=Toxicity of Equisetum to Horses|url= https://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/livestock/horses/facts/07-037.htm|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130929024046/http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/livestock/horses/facts/07-037.htm|archivedate=29 September 2013|accessdate=1 December 2010}}</ref>  

Recent research has shown limited evidence of anti-inflammatory, diuretic, antimicrobial, and antioxidant properties. <ref name="Şeyma Şahinler-2022">{{cite book |last=Şeyma Şahinler |first=Saliha |title=Novel Drug Targets with Traditional Herbal Medicines |publisher=SpringerLink |year=2022 |isbn=978-3-031-07752-4 |pages=249–262 |chapter=Equisetum arvense L |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-07753-1_17 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-07753-1_17 |accessdate=12 October 2022}}</ref>

=== Craft production ===
It was also once used to polish [[pewter]] and wood (gaining the name ''pewterwort'') and to strengthen [[fingernail]]s. It is also an abrasive. It was used by [[hurdy-gurdy]] players to dress the wheels of their instruments by removing resin build up.<ref>La Vielleuse Habile, Jean-Francois Bouin, 1761, p.  19.</ref>

=== Horticultural and agricultural ===
In horticulture and agriculture, an aqueous extract of ''E. arvense'' has been approved for use as a [[fungicide]] in the European Union and the United Kingdom (since Brexit).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Low-risk active substances and basic substances|url=https://www.hse.gov.uk/pesticides/pesticides-registration/applicant-guide/low-risk-active-substances.htm|access-date=2021-11-29|website=www.hse.gov.uk}}</ref> Horsetail extract can be used to prevent fungal [[Pathogen|pathogens]] on crops including:<ref>{{Cite web|last=European Commission|title=Review report for the basic substance Equisetum arvense L. Finalised in the Standing Committee on the Food Chain and Animal Health at its meeting on 20 March 2014 in view of the approval of Equisetum arvense L. as basic substance in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009|url=https://mst.dk/media/171087/review-report-for-equisetum-arvense-l-rev7-vdo.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220703110411/https://mst.dk/media/171087/review-report-for-equisetum-arvense-l-rev7-vdo.pdf|archivedate=2022-07-03}}</ref>

* Damping off (''[[Pythium]]'') and [[powdery mildew]] on cucumbers.
* Various fungal diseases of fruit trees, including scab (''[[Venturia inaequalis]]''), mildew, and [[Leaf curl|peach leaf curl]] (''Taphrina deformans'').
* Both [[Downy mildew|downy]] and powdery mildew on grapevines.
* [[Alternaria solani|Early blight]] (''Alternaria solani'') and Septoria blight (''[[Septoria lycopersici]]'') on tomatoes.
* [[Botrytis cinerea|Grey mould]], powdery mildew, red core, and [[Canker|anthracnose]] fruit rot (''Colletotrichum acutatum'') in strawberries.
* [[Alternaria solani|Early blight]], [[Phytophthora infestans|late blight]], and [[powdery mildew]] on potatoes.

''Equisetum'' is used in [[Biodynamic agriculture|biodynamic farming]] (preparation BD 508) in particular to reduce the effects of excessive water around plants (such as fungal growth). The high silica content of the plant reduces the impact of moisture.<ref name="Kearny">{{cite web|last=Kearny|first=Peter|title=Bio Dynamic Prep 508|url=http://cityfoodgrowers.com.au/bd508.php|work=Bio Dynamic Prep 208|publisher=City Food Growers|accessdate=1 June 2011}}</ref>

=== Traditional medicine ===
''E. arvense'' has been used in traditional [[Austria]]n herbal medicine internally as tea, or externally as baths or compresses, for treatment of disorders of the skin, locomotor system, kidneys and urinary tract, rheumatism and gout.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}

Externally it was traditionally used for [[chilblain]]s and wounds.<ref>Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (Century, 1987); pp. 159–160</ref>

In Finnish traditional medicine, ''E. arvense'' ({{langx|fi|peltokorte}}) has been especially valued for its high concentration of [[silicic acid]] and has been seen to help and been used in a number of ways:

* Green summer shoots, dried, as a remedy.
* Seen as preventing inflammation, strengthening skin and immune system.
* A [[decoction]] of ''E. arvense'' has been used internally to treat all kinds of lung diseases and externally to treat rashes and hard-to-treat wounds.<ref name="Piirainen-1999">{{cite book |last1=Piirainen |first1=Mikko |title=Kotimaan luonnonkasvit |last2=Piirainen |first2=Pirkko |last3=Vainio |first3=Hannele |date=1999 |publisher=WSOY |isbn=951-0-23001-4 |location=Porvoo, Finland |page=497 |language=fi |trans-title=Native wild plants}}</ref>

In Iran, infusion of its shoots is believed to be a remedy against diabetes and obesity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buso |first1=Piergiacomo |last2=Manfredini |first2=Stefano |last3=Reza Ahmadi-Ashtiani |first3=Hamid |last4=Sciabica |first4=Sabrina |last5=Buzzi |first5=Raissa |last6=Vertuani |first6=Silvia |last7=Baldisserotto |first7=Anna |title=Iranian Medicinal Plants: From Ethnomedicine to Actual Studies |journal=[[Medicina (journal)|Medicina]] |date=February 2020 |volume=56 |issue=3 |page=15 |doi=10.3390/medicina56030097|pmid=32110920 |pmc=7143749 |doi-access=free |hdl=11392/2427783 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
